is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,

descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.

- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. There is no proposal inbox; hold an unanswered question in the conversation and continue independent work.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip this for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Build the queue: requirements waiting for approval, designs marked proposed, items at stage 11 waiting for result approval, and Open Questions rows where the owner decides. The command lists each decision once. Its "Agent to-do" lines are the agent's own steps, not decisions waiting on the owner: count and show only the decisions, and handle a delivery offer there with `work-delegate` after the queue.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. The owner gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision. If two could match, ask which one, naming both.
3. Otherwise take the decisions one at a time, the one blocking the most work first. For each: what is being decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue; a bare question is not enough. One decision per message.
4. A requirements approval: save his words as a history note first, so no later session asks him again. Then check the Agreed goal and the open questions. The goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown with the approval question, then record the approval. A requirement still has an open question linked: say which one, open `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval, without asking him again, once it is answered.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>" --effect "Requirements approval to record."`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text "<goal he was shown>"`
5. Record each answer where it belongs. Approvals (for requirements, first set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, as `work-requirements` step 8 does; after it, a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design` unless the owner agreed to skip the design, and a skip is said in the final reply). A design approval also answers an open question that asked for that choice: mark that row Answered.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   An Open Questions answer: rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and status Answered.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --set-file <file>`
   Then, for an approval or an answer: one history note in the owner's words (a requirements approval has it from step 4), and `waiting_on` set to `agent` when the agent continues (the approve command sets it to `none` by itself), unless another question for him on that item is still open.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   A delivery offer listed as an agent to-do: open `work-delegate` once the owner's decisions are done.
6. A decision for the whole project: add a `DECISIONS.md` row and save it with `publish-docs`. Run the command inside the worktree `publish-docs` opens, then let it commit and push.
   `toolkit decision add --decision "<decision>" --why "<why>" --by <owner>`
7. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
8. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. When the queue is empty, say so and offer to continue unblocked items with `work-on`. End the reply with the next decision's question, or the exact words that continue.

## What counts as an answer

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in the history note. The lifecycle command prints the full approval rules:
  `toolkit work lifecycle`
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), or silence is not an answer. Ask again in one line.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- "Yes", "ok", or "looks good" with nothing waiting: ask what he is approving.
- Set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent can continue, to `none` when nothing waits, or keep `owner` when another owner question is still open on that item.

## After a result approval

The item continues with `work-finish` (pull request, deployment, requirements baseline, Done). Open it when the owner wants it shipped now.

## Project-wide decisions

- A decision for the whole project goes in `DECISIONS.md`, not in memory and not in one item. Examples: "use Postgres everywhere", and a standing merge instruction ("agents may merge a pull request after an independent check finds no blocking issue").
- A decision that replaces an older one names it with `--replaces D-<n>`:
  `toolkit decision add --decision "<decision>" --why "<why>" --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>`
- A decision about one item stays in that item: its Recent History, the answered Open Questions row, and Notes > Decisions and context when the next session needs the context.
- `DECISIONS.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or remove a row; a changed decision is a new row that names the one it replaces.

## Tracker notes

- GitHub Issues or Jira: the `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3. Build the queue from the waiting-on-owner and stage 11 labels that `../../references/trackers/github.md` or `../../references/trackers/jira.md` names, and record answers as `../../references/trackers.md` says. Remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer, as above.

# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history, branches) and `references/trackers.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop. When the briefing or a `toolkit work` command lists changes found in the tracker (a moved or renamed folder, a new parent, a missing item), tell the owner each one in one line before other work.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. Setup is not a work item: never create one for setup steps; owner steps go in the reply and in the current focus under "Waiting on the owner". "New work", "track", "work item", or "done properly" always makes an item, and content the owner has not described is a question for him, never a quick edit. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way, titled in the owner's words (say the title in one line), and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --text "<the owner's words>"`
4. A substantial goal whose item shows `delivery: not-offered`: open `work-delegate` first. When it asks the offer, wait for his answer before building. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load`, or the owner answered the questions that set them, or asked for it done properly: `work-requirements`, which shows them to him for approval. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. A `build` item going to planning without a design: say so in the final reply, not a progress line ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me."), and put the reason in a history note. An item that changes committed files goes through stage 07 (its own worktree), never onto the default branch. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the table and checkbox format in this skill's own `references/planning.md` (the `references/` folder beside this `SKILL.md`; read it first). Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's worktree `.claude/worktrees/wi-<number>-<slug>` on branch `claude/wi-<number>-<slug>`; in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. In Codex, `git worktree add`, `git add`, and `git commit` need the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason), because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks. Refused without asking: show him the exact command, ask him to approve it or run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting on the owner. Never work around it (the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, "Branches and worktrees"). With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, and validation is clean. End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "<what changed>"`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

- Each item has one main session that changes it. Other sessions return
  findings to it instead of editing the same record.
- Worktrees keep code apart; they do not keep shared environments apart.
  Check shared orgs, databases, and releases before two items change the same
  one.

## What this design solves

A person running the greet CLI can request an uppercase greeting with --shout. The flag works before or after a supplied name and with no name. Calls without the flag keep their current output. The README shows the new flag.

## Requirements and design readiness

The approved requirements are ready for this small CLI change. No open requirement questions remain.

| Requirement | Status in work item | Design coverage | Remaining decision or gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 — Shout greeting | Finalized | Option A parses the flag and capitalizes the full greeting. | None |
| R-02 — Flag documentation | Finalized | Option A adds a README example. | None |

## What exists today

`bin/greet.mjs` uses the first command-line argument as the name and calls `greet`, which returns `Hello, <name>!` or `Hello, world!`. `test/greet.test.mjs` tests those two function results. The README shows a name example and does not name any flag. These statements were checked in the project files on 2026-09-27.

## Constraints and assumptions

| Type | Constraint or assumption | Source and status | Effect on the design |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Constraint | Keep the current greeting output when --shout is absent. | R-01, approved 2026-09-27 | Apply uppercase only after the normal greeting is formed. |
| Constraint | Accept --shout before or after the name. | R-01, approved 2026-09-27 | Find the flag independently of the name argument. |
| Assumption | Only the placement and outputs named in R-01 are specified. | WI-001 requirements, checked 2026-09-27 | Other argument combinations keep existing handling where practical. |

## Design options

### Option A — Parse the flag in the existing CLI

#### Approach

Keep the existing `greet` function for normal greetings. In the command-line entry point, detect --shout and find the name from the remaining arguments. Capitalize the complete greeting when the flag is present. Add command-line tests and a README example.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. A person runs `node bin/greet.mjs` with an optional name and --shout.
2. The CLI identifies --shout and passes the remaining name, if any, to `greet`.
3. The CLI prints the normal greeting or its uppercase form.

#### Requirement coverage

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why it meets the requirement | How to check it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R-01 | Reuse `greet`; change argument handling in `bin/greet.mjs`. | Uppercase is applied to the entire greeting, and the flag is found in either position. | Run the CLI with --shout Mike, Mike --shout, --shout alone, and without the flag. |
| R-02 | Change `README.md`. | The flag and one invocation with output appear in the README. | Read the README example. |

#### Technical shape

- **Components and files:** Change `bin/greet.mjs` for flag handling; change `test/greet.test.mjs` for CLI checks; change `README.md` for usage.
- **Data and state:** No persistent data or state.
- **Access and security:** The command only processes local command-line arguments.
- **Integrations:** No external integration.
- **Operations:** Run `npm test`; no deployment target is defined.

#### Tradeoffs and risks

| Tradeoff or risk | Likelihood and effect | Mitigation or owner decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Argument parsing could treat --shout as the name. | Directly affects the requested output. | Test both flag positions and the flag alone. |
| Uppercasing only the name would leave Hello mixed case. | Directly violates R-01. | Uppercase the completed greeting and check exact output. |

#### Build order

1. Update argument handling and uppercase output in `bin/greet.mjs`; check the required invocations.
2. Add CLI tests for the required flag positions and unchanged output; run `npm test`.
3. Add a --shout example with output to `README.md`; review it against R-02.

## Recommendation and owner decision

**Recommendation:** Option A. It changes the existing small CLI directly and needs no dependency.  
**Owner decision:** Mike chose Option A on 2026-09-27.

name: work-check
description: 'Checks a finished build against every requirement with an independent checker agent, fixes what fails, then shows the owner the result to approve. Use when the owner asks "is it ready", "does it work", "test it", or "check it against what I asked for", or when a build''s last task is done.'

# Work check

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md` and `references/helpers.md` (how to brief agents), two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line: in Codex a command joined by `&&`, `;`, a pipe, or a heredoc, or run from a script, runs inside the sandbox and fails. Give text with `--text`, or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder (never a fixed `/tmp` name, deleted right after the command). Never change a record with a script.

## Steps

1. Read the requirements, the acceptance list, and the tasks, then set the testing stage. When the show output's "Design:" value is not `none`, also read the design's Acceptance checks (in "Build and verification plan") and the selected option's "How to check it" column (the design command exits 1 for an item with no design). A sub-item whose "Design:" says "none of its own" and names its parent's approved design is checked against that design: read the parent's.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work design <id>`
   `toolkit work design <parent-id>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 09-testing`
2. Run the project's tests and every acceptance check the item lists. A check with several scenarios or manual steps gets a test plan: a copy of `tests/TEST-PLAN-TEMPLATE.md` named for the item, with the results filled in. A check that could not run is reported as not run, never as passed.
3. Brief the `acceptance-checker` agent (never the agent that built it): one verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met) with evidence, plus defects seen in the diff. Give it the branch and commit to check.
4. Failures: set the bug-fixing stage; a `builder` agent (or the main agent) fixes; the checker checks again. Repeat until clean, or until a failure needs an owner decision (an Open Questions row and the item waiting on the owner).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 10-bug-fixing`
5. Record the result: what was checked, the evidence, the known gaps.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Checked: <what>; evidence: <where>; gaps: <gaps or none>"`
6. Set the approval stage and wait on the owner. Show him what it does now, how to see it (a link, a command, or a screenshot), the evidence, and the gaps. Ask one line: "Do you approve this result?"
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 11-user-approval --waiting-on owner`
7. Yes: record it (the command adds its own history row), quote his words in one note, and hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open; then open `work-finish`. A requirement change goes to `work-requirements`; a fix becomes a task and continues here. Every reply ends with the approval question, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker`: step 3 and every re-check. Paste in the Agreed goal, every `R-xx` with its acceptance check, the Acceptance list, the design's Acceptance checks and "How to check it" column, and the test plan when there is one. Name the branch and commit.
- `builder`: fixes in step 4 when a team was recorded or the owner agreed; one builder per independent fix, one writer per path.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Showing the result

- Lead with what the result does now, in the owner's terms: "The export button now creates a CSV file that opens in Excel."
- Then how he can see it himself: the link, the command to run, or a screenshot.
- Then the evidence: tests run and their result lines, the checker's verdicts.
- Then the gaps: anything partly met, not run, or known to be missing. Never hide a gap to get an approval.
- One question: "Do you approve this result?"

## Rules

- The checker is independent: never the agent or session that built the change. When no independent check could run, say so plainly before asking for approval.
- A check that did not run is never reported as passed.
- The approval covers the result shown. It is not an approval to merge, deploy, or publish; `work-finish` handles those.
- "Looks good" to a question other than the approval question is not the approval. Ask the approval question.
- A "no": record his words, turn each named problem into a task or a requirement change, and continue.

---
name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in project memory, and sends anything that belongs elsewhere to its home. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "always do X", "never do X", "forget that", or "remind me", corrects the agent, or a hook says to save.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Put each `toolkit` command on its own line. In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a heredoc) or run from a script runs inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion: run it alone. Text: give it in the command with `--body "<text>"` (a save) or `--text "<text>"` (the focus or the glossary), so no file is needed. For a long text, in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--set-file -` or `--body-file -` with a heredoc); in Codex make a new folder for each save with `mktemp -d`, write the file there, and delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds. Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`: another session could write the same file.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate.
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. There is no proposal inbox: keep an unanswered question in the conversation and go on with other work.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body file with the model's labels: Remember, Why (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), How to apply, Evidence and limits (the source and an absolute date), Related memories (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), Authoritative records. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26" or "requirements/billing.md, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. Giving the same record a better name, or a type that matches its content: rename it; links to it are repaired. Use the first save form when the owner approved (his words or his yes); the second only for a routine save in `trusted` mode.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>" --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description "<one line>" --body-file <file> --source "<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>"`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus, change it, write it back. The model's format: a "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status. On a new project the focus still holds the setup text: remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Declined saves

- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`

toolkit memory: Save, find, and manage project memory: records, the current focus, and the glossary.

  toolkit memory save --type <t> --name <slug> --description <d> (--body <text> | --body-file <file|->)
                      [--approved-by <who>] [--authorization <text>] [--supersedes <key>] [--source <text>]
                      [--status <s>] [--last-verified <YYYY-MM-DD|unknown>] [--expect <version|absent>]
  toolkit memory find <query> [--reflect] [--type <t>] [--limit <n>] [--all]
  toolkit memory get <key>
  toolkit memory list [--type <t>] [--status <current|needs-review|retired|all>]
  toolkit memory retire <key> [--superseded-by <key>] [--reason <text>]
  toolkit memory restore <key>
  toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>
  toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved
  toolkit memory focus [--set-file <file|-> | --text <text>] [--expect <version>]
  toolkit memory glossary [--set-file <file|-> | --text <text>] [--expect <version>]
  toolkit memory reindex
  toolkit memory status
  toolkit memory export --to <folder>
  toolkit memory import --from <folder> [--dry-run]

Types: user, feedback, project, reference, event. A key is <type>_<slug>, for example feedback_deploy_window.
The key is also the file name without .md and the frontmatter name (the model's topic format).
A key typed with dashes (feedback_deploy-window) finds the same record.
A --name longer than 60 characters is refused, not shortened.
A body file that starts with frontmatter fills any field not given as a flag.
--approved-by writes "authorization: Approved by <who> on <date>". With no approver
and memory.approval trusted, it is "Trusted grant"; --authorization sets the words.
Saving over an existing record keeps its source, authorization, supersedes,
last_verified, and any other frontmatter fields unless they are given again.
Saving a record that needs review marks it verified today.
retire --superseded-by <key> marks the record superseded (the replacement must
exist and not be archived); retire alone archives it (built-in: moved to
.memory/archive/). A record saved with status superseded or archived keeps that
word; a superseded record stays beside the current ones.
Links to a note in other notes are repaired when it is renamed (rename, or save
--supersedes), superseded, archived (the link becomes its words plus "(archived)"),
or deleted (the link becomes its words); the notes changed are listed, and so
are notes whose links could not be repaired. Saving an archived note as current
moves it out of archive/ and keeps its links working.
